**Goal.** Add a nonlinear covariate effect to the stage-2 truth, motivated by the authors' Q5 shoaling GAMM. Show what the linear GLMM gets wrong and what a GAM recovers. Smooths are basis functions with a penalty, so this stage also sets up the Hefley framing for stage 4.

## Checklist

- [ ] Q5 motivation: why the authors moved to a GAM
- [ ] Write `sim_nonlinear()` in `sim/sim_nonlinear.R`
- [ ] Fit the (misspecified) GLMM
- [ ] Fit the GAM
- [ ] Ramp: strength of the nonlinearity
- [ ] Reading: Hefley on splines as basis functions

```{r}
#| label: setup
source("../sim/_load.R")
library(glmmTMB)
library(mgcv)
HTrees2 <- read.table(file.path(data_dir, "abundance.only.natural.trees.txt"),
                      header = TRUE, dec = ".")
```

## 1. Q5 motivation

Read `R code/script_question5_shoaling.R` (around lines 51–117) and `output/script_question5_shoaling.txt`. Note what convinced the authors the relationship was nonlinear, the AIC comparison of smooth vs linear terms, and their choice of `s(TreePerimeter)` and a cyclic `s(DistReef, bs = "cc")`.

**Done when:** 3–4 bullet notes, including whether a cyclic smooth in DistReef makes physical sense.

## Diagnostics for the talk

Residuals vs the covariate under the GLMM (where the curvature shows up), and the GAM's partial-effect plot against the truth.

**Done when:** both figures saved to `results/`.

## 5. Reading: smooths are basis functions

Read the parts of Hefley et al. (2017) that treat splines as basis functions. Connect the GAM you just fit to Z α with a penalty. Notes go in `notes/derivations.qmd`.

**Done when:** you can say what Z, α and the penalty are in your GAM.
